claims.text: The proposed baseline material is a powder-metallurgy-processed W-Ta-Cr-V refractory high-entropy alloy.
Approximately 2 at% Hf can be incorporated into the W-Ta-Cr-V alloy with a homogeneous distribution by optimized powder metallurgy.
Optimized powder-metallurgy processing will prevent phase segregation in the Hf-modified alloy.
Adding Hf to W-Ta-Cr-V will induce lattice distortion, local atomic rearrangements, and localized strain fields.
The Hf-induced strain fields will change irradiation-defect migration from long-range anisotropic or one-dimensional motion to short-range isotropic or three-dimensional motion.
Localized three-dimensional motion of interstitial clusters increases vacancy-interstitial recombination.
Greater vacancy-interstitial recombination reduces the formation and growth of voids and defect clusters.
Chemical disorder and lattice distortion in compositionally complex alloys can alter defect formation energies, migration barriers, mobility, and migration paths.
The 2 at% Hf-modified W-Ta-Cr-V alloy will have more than 30% lower void volume fraction than the Hf-free baseline after irradiation.
The Hf-modified alloy will retain yield strength better than the Hf-free baseline after irradiation.
The Hf-modified alloy will retain ductility better than the Hf-free baseline after irradiation.
The proposed benefit will hold under simultaneous approximately 10 keV He+ and approximately 5 keV D+ irradiation at 800-1100 °C.
The radiation-tolerance benefit depends on Hf being uniformly distributed.
Microstructural inhomogeneity or deviations in processing parameters may diminish the benefit of Hf addition.
The effect magnitude may be sensitive to the precise Hf distribution and resulting microstructural features.
Comparing identically processed Hf-free and 2 at% Hf samples under identical dual-beam irradiation provides a controlled test of the intervention.
